newsitem.title: MEXICO: One Mexican leftist killed, one jailed in Oaxaca.
newsitem.headline: One Mexican leftist killed, one jailed in Oaxaca.

text.p: One member of Mexico's main leftist party was murdered in Oaxaca state and another "arbitrarily" arrested there on Saturday, party leaders said.

The opposition Party of the Democratic Revolution (PRD) said the two incidents were part of a campaign by pro-government forces against the PRD in Oaxaca state before congressional elections on July 6.

Augustin Garcia Dominguez, 54, was gunned down in the coastal town of Santa Marta Cortijos, making him the 10th PRD murder victim this year, Flavio Sosa, a PRD federal congressman, said in a statement.
Garcia was killed "after posting party propaganda in Santiago Llano Grande, a neighboring town," the statement, issued Saturday, said.

In addition, local PRD leader Antonio Manuel Garcia "was detained arbitrarily" and held incommunicado by police in Santa Maria Tonameca, a town ruled by the Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI), local PRD leader Saul Vicente said late on Saturday.

The PRI, which has governed Mexico for 68 years, has not commented on PRD claims that the PRI is organizing the attacks, which officials in the Oaxaca state attorney general's office have promised to investigate.
"We ask for the intervention of all human rights organizations who can to come to the coast of Oaxaca and verify the violence and impunity that rule in this region," Sosa said.
"We're sure that these are attacks related to the electoral process ... because the violence started to rise again in March, just before the campaigns started," he said.

The violence in Oaxaca reached a climax on June 4 when four members of a PRD militant's family were gunned down in their home by paramilitary forces while three young children watched, according to the PRD.
Mexico will elect all 500 members of its lower house of Congress, one-fourth of the Senate, six state governments and, for the first time, a Mexico City mayor on July 6.
Political analysts and pollsters say there is a chance the PRI could lose its majority in Congress for the first time since it started its uninterrupted rule in 1929.
